# Attention: Theory, Principles, Models and Applications

Christopher Wickens

Department of Psychology, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, USA

## ABSTRACT

We discuss two general concepts of attention: (1) As a **filter** of selective attention that selects and admits channels of information from the environment to be processed; (2) as a **resource** to enable subsequent information processing, constrained by the individual demand of tasks, and particularly the collective demands of multiple tasks needing to be performed concurrently defining the limits of multitasking. In both concept domains we review theories and design principles, and particularly computational models of attentional process and performance outputs. In discussing the filter we consider supervisory control, noticing, visual search, and the way in which limited selective attention constrains the filter can be overcome to avail more parallel processing via techniques of display overlay and object display. In discussing the fuel for multi-tasking, we distinguish between the parallel processing supported by multiple resources, and the sequential processing and task switching required when demands are excessive.

## 1. Introduction

Engineering Psychology and theory-based human factors strive to derive applications to design and real-world human job performance that are anchored in theories of psychology and ergonomics. This connection between theory and applications is often mediated by two important components both of which will be a focus of this article: **principles of design**, that are useful and usable derivatives of theory, and **models of human performance**, cognition and ergonomics that are intended to actually compute human performance outcomes (accuracy, response times, workload). For example, such models make it possible to compute the predicted human performance benefits of design the principles are adhered to.

The goal of this article is to make this linkage between theories and applications, via principles and models in the context of theories of attention. Such theories, in large part, address human cognition and performance in complex multi-task, or information overload environments. (An exception here are theories of sustained attention, or **vigilance** in underload environments; which we do not address in this article). There are many real-world examples of attention overload: two such examples are the texting driver who causes a collision; or emergency management in the aircraft or at the nuclear power console, where the operator must diagnose a problem, based upon a cacophony of alarms and a Christmas tree of warning lights, and then multi-task, in order to stabilize the system, communicate and further troubleshoot.

In this article, we introduce the theories of attention from which models and principles are derived, within the context of a descriptive model of human attention and performance shown in Figure 1. Such principles, if applied in design, can potentially remediate problems of attention such as those described above. On the left of the figure, multiple dynamic events and more static sources of input in the world are received by the human senses. In turn, this (frequently) large number must be **filtered** by our **selective attention**, so that only the limited number, within our bandwidth limitations can be passed on to the information processing system. Here we perceive (make meaning out of), cognitively process, and ultimately respond to these filtered inputs, in a manner that characterizes basic information processing (Wickens & Carswell, 2021).

Importantly, these processes are often not automatic: they consume limited cognitive resources. If the processing demands are difficult, such as the cognition required to mentally multiply two 2-digit numbers, performance may fail because of these limits. In particular, if **divided attention** between two or more **tasks** is required, in order to “multi-task”, the limited resources will also constrain performance. Just as the filter was seen to define the limits and properties of selective attention, so the metaphor of a limited supply of mental resources can define the limits and properties of divided attention between tasks. This dichotomy between filter and resources characterizes the two main subdivisions of models and principles in this article: those that focus on selective attention between and among input channels, and those that focus on divided attention between tasks. Within each of these, we address major classes of attention-demanding tasks which, in turn, spawn models and principles that can be used to mitigate attention problems when humans interact with technology outside the laboratory.

## 2. Attention filter models

## 2.1. Supervisory control

In many attention-relevant environments, the human operator is confronted with a wide array of dynamic sources of information. We refer to these as **Areas of Interest** or AOIs. Typically, they are human-designed dynamic displays, such as an altimeter, speedometer or pressure indicator, or panel of warning lights, but also may include naturalistic elements like the view down the highway or out the cockpit windscreen, or the area of a surgical patient’s body (Grungeiger et al., 2020; Koh et al., 2011). The goal of the operator here may be to control some of these (e.g., heading in a car, altitude in an aircraft), but also to monitor most or all of them, in case any of these go out of bounds (or are predicted to do so).

Because the eye has a limited field of view of approximately 4 degrees for processing dynamic elements (slightly larger than the fovea), and typical workspaces are far larger, visual scanning is a vital task in such supervision, and human factors engineers would like to predict this scanning behavior, as a proxy for selective attention, for two reasons:

(1) If a particular AOI occupies a large percentage of scan time, even if it contributes little vital information to the user, this can be symptomatic of a poor display layout.

(2) If a particular AOI that **is** important, and perhaps safety-critical, is neglected for a long period of time (e.g., the roadway ahead, while the driver is engaged in head-down scanning), this is an important signal for re-design or training to present such attentional tunneling.

These, and other important aspects of visual supervision can be predicted from a computational model of visual scanning called SEEV (Wickens, 2015; Wickens et al., 2003), constructed on the foundations provided by optimal models of scanning by Senders (1968, 1964) and Sheridan (1970); see also Moray (1986). The model is named for four factors that prominently drive scanning, **Salience, Effort, Expectancy and Value**. More specifically the model predicts that scanning to an AOI can be predicted by the linear weighted sum of these: sS -efEF + exEX + vV, to be described below. The additive combination of these four terms produces a **net attractiveness** of each AOI in the workspace, and, with each iteration of the model, the gaze will travel to each, with a likelihood related to its attractiveness relative to all others, including staying where it is. The lowercase letters in the equation represent weightings, and often these are all set to 1.0 (equal weighting of all terms).

Describing these terms in more detail, historically the oldest is **Expectancy**, related to the bandwidth or event rate of change at the AOI. A higher bandwidth means a greater expectancy of events there, and hence a proportionately greater need to attend (Senders, 1964; Carbonell et al., 1968). Thus, for example, when driving on a straight, uncrowded highway, the expectancy of events is low, and the gaze can be free to safely wander away from the forward view for a short duration. But on a curvy highway with lots of traffic, the high resulting bandwidth requires a great deal of scanning out the windshield AOI. Optimal sampling theory dictates that an AOI should be sampled at half the bandwidth in order to fully reconstruct the signal (Moray, 1986).

**Value** was added to an optimal scanning model by Sheridan (1970). This term is directly related to the value of sampling an AOI, or the cost of not sampling it. The safety cost when driving, of not looking at the roadway AOI is obvious, just as is the very low value of sampling an advertising sign beside the roadway. Given that tasks can be assigned importance, the SEEV model states that the value of an AOI is equal to the **importance** of the task multiplied by the **degree of relevance** of the AOI to the task (Wickens, 2015). Whereas expectancy can be objectively measured from the event rate or bandwidth, determination of value requires a subjective call by the modeler. However, there is often consensus, for example, in driving, that the value of sampling the roadway, is greater than that of sampling the speedometer. In flying, the value of sampling instruments to stabilize the aircraft, is greater than the value of sampling a navigational display (Schutte & Trujillo, 2017)

Importantly, the product of expectancy and value defines the **expected value** of looking at each AOI, and hence characterizes what should be the **optimal scan path** for supervisory control. Yet this scan path is thwarted by two “nuisance factors”, the other two terms of SEEV that are known to drive visual attention. The role of **Salience** is intuitive. Large bright, high contrast AOIs tend to dominate our gaze: consider the large flashing roadside advertisement billboard. But it is a nuisance variable in that it should not exert that dominance unless it is intentionally made by the designer to correlate with value. Like expectancy, salience has been objectively quantified by a visual salience model proposed by Itti and Koch (2000), and has often been validated in subsequent years. Although the original model is incomplete, not accounting for dynamic salience, this feature can be added via a straightforward technique (Steelman et al., 2013; Steelman et al., 2016).

**Effort** here is operationally defined as the muscular effort required to move the scan from one AOI to another. Hence, in contrast to Ex, V and S, effort is a property of AOI **pairs** (Eisma et al., 2018; Wickens, 2014). Also, unlike the other three terms, it is an inhibitory, negative force, rather than an attractive one. Effort can be objectively measured as a linear function of the visual angle between all pairs of AOIs. A simple heuristic for effort imposes a constant slope, as shown in Figure 1 (solid line). However, a more realistic function imposes two slopes (dashed line): when the separation of AOIs is less than about 20 degrees, the slope is low, because only an eye scan is needed to move fixation from one to the other, and rotation of the eyeball is a low-inertia action. However, moving visual attention more than around 20 degrees is often coupled with head movement (a neck rotation) which is more effortful, and hence imposes a steeper slope (cost/unit of visual angle; Wickens, 1993; Wickens & McCarley, 2008). The predicted higher effort in scanning across a workspace leads to higher rated subjective workload (Eisma et al., 2018).

In sum then, the additive combination of these four terms, S – Ef + EX + V, when equally weighted, and when each is standardized on a 0–1 (minimum to maximum) scale can predict a stochastic scan pattern. At each model iteration, the net attractiveness of all AOIs is calculated (with greater effort inhibiting attractiveness), including the attractiveness of that AOI which is hosting the current fixation. The scan path then moves to an AOI with a probability in proportion to its attractiveness. Since the effort of “moving” to the current AOI is 0, the effort factor will slightly favor an iteration that maintains attention for a longer dwell time.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 1. A descriptive information processing model, highlighting two forms of attention.

The model will then generate an NXN transition matrix of the form shown in Table 1, where N is the number of AOIs. Here N = 3. The entries in the cells (u-z) indicate the number of eye movement transitions from the AOI across the top of the matrix, to that down the side of the matrix. Consecutive “self-transitions” in cells along the negative diagonal, u, w and z represent longer dwells (e.g., for a more high-valued AOI). The sum in each column represents the total “net attractiveness” of each AOI. That is, the total number of times that the scan lands on the AOI regardless of its origin. When these numbers are converted to percentages or the proportion of dwell time (DT) at each AOI, this reflects the relative attractiveness of each AOI.

Furthermore, if the model is run as a discrete simulation, data on what is called the “**first passage time**” (Moray, 1986) can inform the distribution of times during which an AOI is **not** fixated, and hence the scanner may be vulnerable to some form of **attentional tunneling**. More details on how to implement the model computationally, as well as a simpler equation version of the model, can be found in Wickens (2015).

Importantly, predictions of the SEEV model have been validated in many real-world contexts including health care (Grungeiger et al., 2020; Koh et al., 2011), the automobile (Horrey, Wickens & Consalus, 2006), the flight deck (Steelman-Allen et al., 2011; Wickens et al., 2003), robotic supervision (Wickens, Sebok et al., 2015); and general supervisory control (Eisma et al., 2018). Such validation is accomplished by correlating the SEEV-predicted PDTs with the % scans or **percentage dwell time (PDT**) on each AOI. It has been used both to predict the overall scanning behavior of users, but also, in some circumstances, to characterize the differences between novice and expert scan patterns (Grungeiger et al., 2021; Koh et al., 2011; Wickens & McCarley, 2008). An important difference here is that experts should be more calibrated to the true expected value of an AOI, and less “distracted” or influenced by the two nuisance parameters of salience and effort.

Finally, we highlight the relevance of SEEV to designing the optimal display layout: a principle that dictates **correlating salience with value, and expectancy with effort**. That is, where the designer has options to position displays (AOIs) within an interface, those which are progressively more valuable (e.g., higher priority alerts and those displays relevant to the most important tasks) should be progressively more salient (a principle already adhered to in guidance for alert design; Federal Aviation Administration, 2011); and **pairs** of displays that are used progressively more frequently (expectancy) should be positioned closer together, in order to minimize overall scanning effort between them. Then, a SEEV model version can be run twice, with, and then without, the two nuisance parameters expectancy and value. To the extent that layout is more optimally, this will produce a progressively smaller difference between these two predicted outputs of the PDT distribution across AOIs.

The SEEV model itself provides a foundation for two further models of attention, which we describe as follows.

## 2.2. From supervision to situation awareness: The A-SA (attention-situation awareness) model

In many environments, such as aviation, the purpose of scans is to sample a dynamic variable, and then maintain awareness of that variable state, after the scan has gone elsewhere. The pilot may scan the altimeter, then look elsewhere for a while before checking the altimeter again. In the duration of this first-passage-time, the variable may have changed its state, or the user’s memory of its value may have decayed, sometimes with disastrous consequences if the scan does not return soon.

Based upon Sheridan’s (1970) original model of “how often a supervisor should sample”, a version of SEEV was produced in which a decay parameter of state estimation can model a degradation of state knowledge over time. This decay, coupled with a model of statistical properties of critical events that can be seen only on the AOI in question (e.g., a hazard in the roadway ahead; Wickens & McCarley, 2008), can be used to predict the likelihood of an attentional error or noticing failure, a model that has received some validation in an aviation context (Wickens & McCarley, 2008) and in the context of monitoring automation (Wickens, Sebok et al., 2015).

## 2.3. From supervision to noticing. The NSEEV model

In the midst of routine supervisory control scanning, a sudden discrete visual event may occur somewhere in the work space, such as the pedestrian unexpectedly entering the roadway, or the red light of an engine overheat alert. Such events should be noticed as soon as possible. Yet a large body of psychological research indicates that people often do not notice them, a phenomenon known as “change blindness” (Rensink, 2002; Simons & Chabris, 1999; Wickens & Alexander, 2009) or “inattentional blindness”. The former term refers to a failure to notice wherever the change event is in the visual field; the latter term specifically applies to an event or change which was within foveal vision at the time it occurred.

Ample research in visual attention indicates that noticing such changes is heavily related to both **expectancy** and **salience** (e.g., Steelman et al., 2013; Rensink, 2002; Steelman-Allen et al., 2011; Wickens, 2009). In addition, visual change detection is clearly inhibited by nonvisual **cognitive load** (Fougnie & Marois, 2007), reflecting the limited information-processing resources within the brain of Figure 1. A fourth factor that is vitally important in change or event detection is the **retinal eccentricity**, in visual angle, between the momentary fixation when the change or visual event occurs, and the location of that event (Wickens et al., 2016). In a controlled laboratory setting, such eccentricity can be carefully controlled by requiring fixation on a “fixation cross” when the event is presented, at different eccentricities to the side, above or below. However, in the dynamic work environment fixations will vary (as predicted by SEEV), so eccentricity is never constant.

This variability can be accounted for however. As shown in Figure 3, which presents a scan path between three AOIs, SEEV can predict the likelihood that the scan will rest in each AOI. Hence, as represented by the thin red lines, SEEV can predict the **distribution of eccentricities** to the location of the “event”, here a warning light that turns on at the location of the red star. Smaller eccentricities, as from the AOI on the lower right, will predict a more rapid detection. Hence if that AOI is particularly “attractive”, such as might be the case for the moving horizon display in a cockpit, the overall distribution of eccentricities will favor the smaller eccentricity, and a faster noticing time, averaged over all AOIs, will be predicted.

Together then, these four factors – expectancy, salience, cognitive load and eccentricity – when combined in an additive fashion are found to produce a fairly accurate prediction of noticing times, when eccentricity itself is driven by the SEEV model output. Hence this model has been referred to as the N-SEEV model of noticing (Steelman et al., 2013; Steelman et al., 2016; Steelman-Allen et al., 2011). A further assumption can be added that, if the event is **not** predicted to be noticed following some criterion time limit after its occurrence (e.g., 5 seconds), it either will not be noticed at all (because its internal visual representation has decayed from memory), or the noticing will be assessed to be impermissibly late; and hence classified as a **missed event**. Where-ever this criterion is placed, will then generate a predicted miss-rate of critical events.

It should be noted that the parameters of NSEEV overlap with those of SEEV, but with important differences. Salience in NSEEV refers to the salience of an **event in time**, not of a region in space. Expectancy refers to the expectancy of the one critical event at one specific location, not the frequency with which multiple events occur at all AOIs. Eccentricity refers to the specific separation between that one event location and all AOIs, in contrast to effort in SEEV, which is measure between pairs of AOIs. But the metric of both effort and eccentricity is in units of visual angle.

In addition to validation of the NSEEV model with simplified aviation simulations (Steelman et al., 2013; Steelman-Allen et al., 2011), a more recent application has applied NSEEV to model the **automation complacency** of operators of a realistic NASA robotics arm simulation (Wickens, Sebok et al., 2015), complacency referring to the excessive withdrawal of scanning from a process controlled by automation, as a result of too much trust in that automation (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010). Here the critical visual event to be noticed is the consequence of a programming coordinates error that sends the arm on an errant trajectory toward a collision. The model accurately pre-dicts the failure in noticing this automation failure.

## 2.4. Visual search and clutter

Supervisory control and the SEEV model address episodes of continuous monitoring and control when no single specific event is defined. Noticing and NSEEV address a specific **event in time** within the context of continuous monitoring of a dynamic environment. A third visual attention task, **visual search**, is related to, but distinct from both of the above in that the environment in which the search takes place need not be dynamic, and the target is a **thing in space**, rather than an event in time. Examples of visual search in the workplace are numerous, including searching a manuscript for typos, a cluttered computer screen for a particular icon, a circuit board for a flaw, a medical image for an abnormality or a cluttered map for a destination. Typically, the most important variable is the time required to find the target residing amongst a background of what are considered “**non-targets**” or **distractors**. For example, the time required to go head down in a moving vehicle and search for a destination on a map is of vital safety concern. But accuracy is also sometimes important, as when, for example, considering the radiologist’s search for polyps in an X-ray image.

Multiple factors, shown in Table 2 (Wickens & McCarley, 2008) influence search time; and probably the most important of these are properties of the search field, (the number of targets, distractors, and background clutter), and the discriminability between targets and distractors.

Several computational models of visual search have been proposed and well-validated, many based upon the original Sternberg (1966) **serial self-terminating search** model. This model proposes that, for many search tasks, search time is a linearly increasing function of the number of distractors (N), and this function doubles in slope in a search task when the target is absent compared to one when the target is present. This doubling results because, on average, if a target is present, it will be found halfway through, so long as items are examined one at a time; but to establish if the target is absent, the entire search field must be examined, one item at a time.

However, the positive slope is only observed when it is hard to discriminate the target from the distractors. In contrast, when it is easy, and the target can be discriminated by the presence of a single salient feature, like a red (enemy) symbol in the midst of non-red items on a military map, then the search is essentially **parallel**. That is, all items are examined at the same time, and search time is unrelated to N; a condition creating a “flat slope” and the so-called “pop out” effect, as the target pops out of the search field. The Sternberg model or a derivative of it has often been employed to predict search times (Wickens & McCarley, 2008). It has been elaborated to generate the most comprehensive and widely used search model called Guided Search (Wolfe, 2007; Wolfe & Horowitz, 2017), which also includes treatments of knowledge-driven or “top-down” expectancy factors in the search process.

As described above, search time is heavily affected by N and target-distractor confusability, but also increased by the **clutter** in the search field, an intuitive concept for all of us, and one that has benefitted from many efforts to quantify it (Moacdieh & Sarter, 2014; Alexander & Kaber, Beck et al., 2010; Rosenholtz et al., 2007; Yeh, & Wickens, 2001a). The visual search paradigm described above has been critical in evaluating many of the models and metrics of clutter in assessing the time to find targets against backgrounds of various kinds and amount of clutter. Here the model proposed by Rosenholtz et al. (2007) and Rosenholtz (2017) has proven particularly useful in identifying and quantifying features that independently contribute to clutter.

One objective of such clutter modeling is for a computer image analysis to be able to objectively quantify the clutter of a scene by extracting measures of the features known to contribute to clutter-based slowing of search. A second objective is to be able to predict the benefit of automation to counter the slowing effects of both clutter and N, and to guide selective attention to an automation-suspected target via through some form of **cueing** (e.g., a reticle surrounding a suspected target; Yeh et al., 2003; Yeh & Wickens, 2001b;

Yeh et al., 1999), an arrow pointing to it (Wickens & Rose, 2001) or highlighting (St. John et al., 2005). Such guidance can be extremely helpful in shortening search time. However, it is only as useful as the **reliability** of the cue-guiding algorithm in inferring what actually is the target (Yeh & Wickens, 2001b). If its reliability is less than 1.0, it will occasionally direct attention to something that is not a wanted target, or fail to direct attention to a true target. In combination, these two types of attention-direction error can sometimes have severe consequences (Yeh et al., 2003). Lee and MacGregor (1985) have developed a model to predict the usefulness (search time saved) of imperfect target cueing.

## 2.5. Display location: The HUD, the HMD and database overlay: From selective to divided attention

The selective attention costs of display separation, expressed by the effort component of SEEV (Figure 2) and the eccentricity component of NSEEV have been mitigated by two closely related design concepts: the **head-up display** (HUD) and the **head-mounted** (sometimes called wearable) display (HMD). The objective of these two techniques is to bring displayed information upward, so that it overlays the view of an “outside world” where important task-relevant information is also to be found, hence, ideally, turning what was once a sequential selective attention challenge (look at the display OR the outside world) into a divided attention or parallel processing benefit: attend to both the near (display) and far domains simultaneously (Wickens et al., 2004). A closely related technique is referred to as **database overlay**, in which several aspects of geographical information are overlaid on a single map, rather than displayed adjacently (Kroft & Wickens, 2003; Wickens, 2000). Thus, a pilot’s dynamic digital map may contain overlaid information regarding weather, air traffic, terrain and air routes (Kroft & Wickens, 2003).

HUDs have been long used in many aircraft, particularly in the military, and are increasingly seen in automobiles, while HMDs have seen uses in many domains such as health care, industry and military ground operations (Dey et al., 2018).

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 3. A SEEV-predicted scan path between three AOIs, coupled with a discrete event (warning light onset) at the location of the red star. The red lines characterize the visual eccentricity between each AOI and the location of the warning light.

While the benefits of such overlaid imagery are intuitive and appealing, it can impose one substantial cost, discussed in the previous section: **clutter**. Here the form of cutter is slightly different from that discussed above, and may be described here as **overlay clutter**. This effect can be revealed by examining the four images in Figures 4 and 5. In Figure 4 is depicted schematically what might be a traditional separated display for a ground vehicle or low flying helicopter. The visual scene is depicted above, and the user looks down to see a top-down map of the geographical features that were viewed directly in the forward view.

In order to mitigate the sequential viewing and selective attention costs in Figure 4, the designer has now moved the display imagery to a head-mounted display shown in the left image of Figure 5. The HMD contains two qualitatively different types of imagery: **non-conformal** or **screen-referenced** imagery, like the digital text at the bottom, and **conformal** or **world-referenced** imagery, like the mountain markers and their identity tags, that overlay their real-world counterparts, and will move across the display in synchrony with any head movements. In many applications this conformal imagery is defined as augmented reality. On the right of Figure 5 is a corresponding head-up display (HUD), for an aircraft approaching a landing. This again reveals the distinction between the non-conformal digital text, and two aspects of conformal imagery: the horizon line, which will rotate as the plane banks in order to stay superimposed over the true horizon, and the small runway overlay.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 4. Schematic example of a separated head down display.

The effects of overlay clutter are illustrated in Figure 5, because some elements of the far domain may be difficult to perceive if overlaid by strokes on the superimposed imagery: note the small symbol hidden behind the digits “315”. Correspondingly, perception of some items in the display, particularly the small green highway label at the base of the mountains may be hindered by complex imagery directly behind it, in the outside world. Similarly, clutter effects of both near and far domain imagery could disrupt the focus of attention in the HUD, to the right. Not surprisingly, the larger and more salient the display imagery, the more it will hinder perception in the far domain, and the less its perception will be hindered **by** far domain clutter.

Thus, overlaying displays may be seen as imposing a tradeoff between two conflicting forces in human performance: the **advantages of reduced scanning**, and the **advantage of reduced clutter** which can be seen by comparing the overlaying images in Figure 5a left, with that in Figure 4, where the small building is quite visible.

Which of these two conflicting forces dominates? This issue was addressed, in aircraft HUDs in a meta-analysis by Fadden et al. (2000; see also Fadden Ververs & Wickens, 2001) who found that overall the benefits of the HUD for encouraging divided attention and parallel processing dominated the costs of clutter, in terms of both flight path tracking performance and display processing. However, this overall advantage was moderated by two important features of the display and task: **conformality** and **information integration** respectively.

When there is conformal imagery, or augmented reality, the common motion of the near domain symbology and its far domain counterpart “links” the two items together as the head or vehicle rotates and fosters the parallel processing of the two, as if belonging to the same object. This linking has its basis in the **object-based theory** of attention (Chen, 2012; Kahneman & Treisman, 1984; Wickens & McCarley, 2008);

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 5. Left: Schematic of an HMD overlay, depicting the information in Figure 4. Right: An aircraft HUD. Both imaged include both conformal and non-conformal imagery as described in the text.

and the benefits of HUD overlay are found to be amplified with conformal imagery (Fadden et al., 2000).

The second, modulating factor of image overlay pertains to the **task performed** on near and far domain information. To illustrate this, we introduce the example of database overlay, in Figure 6.

The clutter effects of all four database, traffic, terrain, weather and air routes, overlaid in the left panel are evident, compared to the right, in which they are separated into two pairs.

Thus considering the task effect, in the context of both database (Figure 6) and image (Figures 4 and 5) overlay, if the task is one of **the focused attention**, such as detecting an uncued target in the far domain (the small building in Figures 4 and 5), reading an instrument on the near domain display, or, in the case of database overlay, searching for an item on one of the databases, like a traffic aircraft, then the benefit of overlay will be reduced, and may actually be reversed because of the costs of overlay clutter. This reversal is particularly evident for the detection of small, unexpected items in the far domain (Fadden et al., 2001, 2000; Yeh et al., 2003). However, if the task is one of **information integration** and divided attention, such as a pilot controlling the airplane to superimpose the HUD-displayed runway over the far-domain runway; or, in the case of data-base integration, assessing if a diversion around weather (one database) will bring a flight path close to nearby traffic or terrain (other databases), then the benefits of overlay are enhanced (Fadden et al., 2000), Kroft and Wickens (2001, 2003, 2000). This is an expression of the more general **proximity-compatibility-principle** in display layout and design (Wickens & Carswell, 1995; Wickens & McCarley, 2008): Information sources to be integrated should be positioned in close proximity. Those for which focused attention is desired, should be positioned farther apart.

There does not exist a formal computational model to predict the relative benefits (or costs) of superimposing images (for HUDs, HMDs and AR). However, the foundations of such a model can be provided by integrating the continuous costs of information access effort for more separated displays, such as shown in Figure 2, (see also Wickens et al., 2005), with an overlay clutter model (yet to be developed; but partially driven by existing clutter models). Such a model should also mitigate overlay clutter costs by a discrete conformality benefit and an information integration benefit, if either of these latter two features are present in the suite of displays and tasks confronting the user.

## 2.6. Divided attention in the filter: The object display

The special benefits of divided attention and parallel processing across the attributes of a single object, which have emerged from object-based theory of attention (Chen, 2012; Kahneman & Treisman, 1984) have also spawned important applications of the object display to represent multi-dimensional data. These include such concepts as the “glyph” or hexagon or octagon display for multi-parameter safety displays in the process control industry (Woods et al., 1981), multi-dimensional icons for weather parameter observations across a geographical region, **Ecological Interface Displays** for complex system understanding (Bennett et al., 2015; Burns, 2013) and the preferred use of line graphs over bar graphs for complex data (the line connecting two points representing a single object, in contrast to the two objects representing the same data in a bar graph, Wickens & McCarley, 2008). When carefully designed, such object displays can be particularly advantageous for information integration tasks, as discussed in the previous section (Wickens & Carswell, 1995; Wickens & McCarley, 2008).

Figure 6. Data-base overlay (left panel) versus separation (right panels). From Kroft and Wickens (2001).

## 2.7. Divided attention in the filter: Human-automation collaboration

Display proximity and objectness can both encourage divided attention. Nowhere can this goal be more important than in **human-automation teaming** in which both agents are tasked with making a judgment based on a common source of data (Getty et al., 1995; Meyer, 2004). A simple example is an alarm system to aid the human in monitoring a dynamic system for a dangerous state. A more complex example is automatic target recognition (ATR) when both agents examine the same image to decide if it represents a target (e.g., a tumor, a smuggled weapon, a hostile actor, a potential aircraft conflict) or not (Foroughi et al., 2019). When such systems are implemented, the effective human member of the team will allocate attention to the process under supervision in a manner that is appropriately **calibrated** to the reliability of that automation (Dixon & Wickens, 2006; Foroughi et al., 2019; Hegerth et al., 2016; Moray, 2003). That is, the calibrated human will scan the automationassisted process proportionately more, as the automation makes more errors in its classification, in order to detect those errors when they occur.

Using a relatively simple regression model, with weights based on a meta-analysis, Wickens and Dixon (2007) found that such calibration was reasonably good, so long as automation reliability remained above about 80%; but was found wanting when automation erred more frequently. Effective design can achieve more accurate calibration by supporting more parallel processing of the automation output and the raw data that are processed by automation. This goal can, in turn, accomplish this by close positioning of the two sources of information (reducing effort), integrating the automation output with the display of the raw data, or, perhaps using a nonvisual modality to present that output, an issue we address in the next section.

In concluding section B, the filter of selective attention incorporates several different processes, whereby visual information input is sometimes driven by the selection of and focus on a small number of items, and sometimes driven by the mental integration, across a larger number of items. This integration can be encouraged by certain techniques (object displays, display overlay) that can transform a limited selective attention, to a more productive divided attention that enables parallel processing. These processes have mostly been captured by theory-driven computational models. Once “admitted” through the input filter of selective attention, further processing by perception, cognition and action is also constrained by attention – now represented by the limited processing resources that particularly constrain divided attention between tasks; that is, **multi-tasking**. These resources too can exhibit both productive concurrent parallel processing, and more inhibiting sequential processing. We address both the successes and restrictions in turn, in the following two parts of section C.

## 3. Attention in multi-tasking

## 3.1. Concurrent multi-tasking

As noted, at the outset of this article, multi-tasking is heavily constrained by the limited cognitive resources that can be deployed to a task. When attempting to perform two tasks concurrently, such limits are represented by **Multiple Resource theory** (Navon & Gopher, 1979; Wickens, 1980, 1984, 2002), which postulates three fundamental elements dictating how well a given task will be performed concurrently with another.

## 3.1.1. Resources and effort

First, most intuitively, the difficulty or attentional resource demand of both tasks will influence time sharing. Easier tasks (those of lower mental workload, or greater **automaticity)** will be time shared more effectively (Kahneman, 1973). The role of resources in improving task performance can be depicted by the **performance-resource function** (Norman & Bobrow, 1975), as depicted in Figure 7.

The figure depicts performance of a task, B, on the Y axis, represented by the dashed line. As more resources are given to it (X-axis) via greater effort invested in its performance or “trying harder”), task B performance improves, although often in a non-linear fashion as shown here. If the task is to be time-shared with another (Task A), whose performance, as a function of the relative resource allocation to A vs B is represented by the solid vertical line, performance on both tasks will be diminished by the need to share these hypothetical mental resources. However, when time sharing, performers have some discretion in allocating resources to, or “favoring”, one task or the other, and the figure depicts two different allocation policies by the two vertical lines. Because of the non-linearity of the performance resource function for task B, the figure suggests that **optimal allocation** will be achieved by the vertical dashed line which, in contrast to the solid line, substantially improves A’s performance, without much degrading B’s performance.

The viability of the resource concept, as an actual “energizer” or fuel in the brain in the mobilization of mental effort, is established by the several neurophysiological correlates, which point to the actual metabolism of blood glucose by the brain, as it carries out its “mental work” (Ayez & Dehaise, 2018). Such metabolic function can be revealed by various physiological measures to assess mental workload (Longo & Leva, 2007, Wickens & Tsang, 2014; Young et al., 2015; Hancock et al., 2021).

The resource concept plays an important role in understanding skill development and instruction. Regarding skill development, the important distinction between skill-based, rule-based, and knowledge-based performance (Rasmussen, 1986) is one that describes both the cognitive processes used as a complex skill is mastered and, as well, the resourcedemands imposed be exercising the skill, progressing from heavily resource limited performance (curve A of Figure 7) to more efficient data-limited performance (Curve B). Researchers have described the latter category as representing the **automaticity** of a highly practiced and learned skill (Fisk, Ackerman & Schneider, 1987). Regarding instruction, **cognitive load theory** (Paas & van Gog, 2009) describes the manner in which limited cognitive resources are allocated among components of a learning environment, and the theory pre-scribes instructional design principles that will optimize the allocation of resources to maximize learning and training.

Figure 7. Transition matrix between three AOIs. For the purposes of computing AOI attractiveness, as described in the text, the three cells in the upper right can be left blank.

## 3.1.2. Multiplicity of resources

Regarding the second element of multiple resource theory, ample research has documented that multi-tasking is not constrained as if all tasks competed for a common pool of **undifferentiated resources**. For example, both intuition and data inform that it is a lot easier (and less dangerous) to drive and converse with a passenger (successful multitasking), than to drive while texting. This is, then, as if the brain possesses multiple resources, with more facile multi-tasking supported when different resources are deployed (Salvucci & Taatgen, 2011; Wickens, 2002; Wickens et al., 2003). These resources appear to be defined by processing code (verbal or linguistic versus spatial), processing stages (perceptual–cognitive operations versus response operations), perceptual modality (visual versus auditory and versus tactile), and visual subsystems (focal vision, required for object recognition, versus ambient vision, required for orientation and locomotion; Previc, 1998).

Each of these dichotomies of resources can be elaborated. For example, to illustrate code-interference, it is because of the separate spatial and verbal code resources that spatially guided manual responses may be more effectively time shared than vocal responses when operators must concurrently rehearse verbal material. Conversely, vocal responses will be more effective than spatially guided manual ones when the operator must concurrently perform another spatial task, such as tracking (e.g., the disruption of driving caused by the spatial keypresses of cell phone dialing, Caird et al., 2018;

Collet et al., 2010). As another example of code interference, the spatial cognitive processes involved in navigation and vehicle control are better time shared with the verbal representation of a memorized verbal route list than with the spatial representation of a memorized map.

It is because of the separate stage-defined resources that we are often able effectively to time share responding operations (e.g., talking) with perceptual ones (e.g., scanning).

It is because of the separate perceptual resources that designers have chosen to offload the heavy visual processing load of vehicle drivers or pilots with some information presented on auditory channels (Wickens et al., 2003), and sometimes tactile channels (Sarter, 2013). A detailed meta-analysis of multi-modal input design has documented the degree of benefit of deploying tactile and auditory displays, rather than visual ones, in the context of an ongoing visual task like driving (Lu et al., 2013).

Finally, it is because of the separate visual channels that we can fairly effectively keep a car centered in the lane (using ambient vision) while searching for and reading road signs or glancing downward to search a navigation display (a task requiring focal vision; Horrey & Wickens, 2006).

Consistent with the neurophysiological mechanisms underlying the resource concept as described above, the categories underlying all four dimensions of the multiple resources are themselves undergirded by neurophysiological distinctions: Spatial versus verbal processing, by right and left cerebral hemispheres respectively; perceptual-cognitive versus response activities by more posterior versus anterior brain regions respectively; visual, auditory and tactile processing by cortical regions, and the ambient versus focal visual channels by dorsal versus ventral neural pathways respectively (Previc, 1998; Wickens, 2008; Wickens et al., 2013).

The third element in predicting success or failure in divided attention between concurrently performed tasks is the **resource allocation policy** between them (Navon & Gopher, 1979; Norman & Bobrow, 1975), as we described above in the context of Figure 7. This feature, allocation policy, accounts for why cell phone and text users in cars do not suffer more accidents than they do: Most drivers still do treat lane-keeping and hazard monitoring as a task of higher priority than that of phone conversation, and hence allocate more resources toward the former. One key factor influencing allocation policy that is beginning to receive research interest is that of “engagement” (Horrey et al., 2017). Engaging and interesting tasks will receive the majority of resources, when time-shared, at the expense of a concurrent task that may, in fact, be of higher priority. A challenge in research is how to predict and assess this engagement level in circumstances where it may compromise safety.

There is one final factor not accommodated by multiple resource theory that can account for differences in the effectiveness of concurrent task performance. This is **confusion**, caused by the similarity of elements within the two tasks (Wickens et al., 2013). The more similar those elements are, the more likely there will be **cross-talk** between the two, such that, for example, elements of one task show up in the response to the other task. A classic example relates to the challenge of patting your head while rubbing your stomach. Another might be trying to tally or copy student test scores while listening to basketball scores. Note, however, that similarity-based confusion is most likely to occur when the tasks already share some demand for common resources (e.g., in the above two examples, both spatial manual tasks or both auditory/verbal tasks using digits).

A computational model to predict the joint influence of resource demand and resource conflict has been developed (Sarno & Wickens, 1995; Wickens, 2002a, 2005, 2008) and has been validated against both data from a simulated multi-tasking flight environment (Sarno & Wickens, 1995) and multitask driving in a high fidelity simulator (Horrey & Wickens, 2003).

This computational multiple resource model consists of two summed components: One, a **demand component** itself sums the overall resource demand of each task in a dual task pair. Such demand values will be derived from measures of single task mental workload. The second, the **multiple resource-conflict component** is more complex. The task pair is examined from the perspective of each of the first three resource-dimensions in turn (codes, stages and modalities), to assess the extent to which the two tasks compete for the common level on each dimension. Thus, for example, the pair of two visual-spatial tasks – monitoring both a continuously changing altimeter and a pressure reading – would have a resource conflict score of two (modalities and codes), so long as one was responded to with voice, and the other with a joystick. If both were responded to with a Joystick (or both by voice), the score would jump to three. This resource conflict score then ranges from 0 to 3. When the mental workload demand scale also is standardized so that 0 is minimum and 3 is maximum, then the sum of the two components can provide an overall, predicted, task interference measure ranging from 0 to 6.

## 3.2. Sequential performance & task management

Even when an operator may try to perform two tasks in parallel (albeit with degraded performance on one or both), this concurrent processing, addressed by multiple resource theory, may become impossible either because one or both are of very high resource demand or because they compete for common incompatible resources, like speaking two different messages at once (the voice can speak only one message at a time), or looking to two sources of widely spaced visual inputs. In these circumstances, once the limits of multiple resources have dictated that concurrence is impossible, multi-tasking now regresses to from a parallel to a serial/sequential mode, and the first two elements of multiple resource theory (demand and resource structure) no longer play a role in predicting interference. Indeed, the early history of attention research was dominated by a view that much of human performance **was** serial, as if passing through a single channel bottleneck (Broadbent, 1958; Welford, 1967).

So, in the high demand circumstances when resource sharing is impossible, the third element of multiple resource theory – allocation policy – now occupies center stage as the most important factor in sequential task management: which tasks are performed and which are completely suspended or neglected, and for how long.

Two general scenarios underlie the manifestation of sequential task management strategies, both involving a **decision process** of which task to perform, and both partially embedded within the framework of queuing theory (Moray et al., 1991; Liu, 2013). One of these is the study of **task switching & management** (e.g. Gonzales & Mark, 2004; Raby & Wickens, 1994; Wickens, Gutzwiller & Santamaria, 2015). The other, really a subset of task management is the study of **interruption management** (e.g., Bailey & Konstan, 2006; Loukopopolous et al., 2009; Trafton & Monk, 2007), a concept that has seen a large focus of research in human-computer interaction. In task-switching paradigms, the operator is confronted with two or more tasks and must choose one to initiate first. In interruption management, the operator is already performing one (the “ongoing task” – OT) when a second task (the “interrupting task” – IT) arrives, and must decide whether (or for how long) to continue the OT before switching to the IT, then when to return to the OT. This might describe the knowledge worker on a computer, interrupted by a phone call. Here researchers often focus on the quality of OT upon return (e.g., how fast it is resumed, whether it is resumed where it was “left off,” etc. Trafton & Monk, 2007; Wickens et al., 2021).

In both task and interruption management, queuing theory can sometimes be applied to determine optimal strategies of task (and interruption) management (Liao & Moray, 1993; Moray et al., 1991). Some of these strategies are quite intuitive, such as when two tasks differ in their importance (or penalty for delayed completion), the more important should be undertaken first. However, when a large number of task features vary between the two tasks, such as their expected duration, their difficulty, the decay of information within a task while it is neglected, or the uncertainty in priority, then assessing optimal solutions becomes very complex. Indeed, in these circumstances it can easily be argued that the mental workload (and time) cost of a human computing the optimal strategy will consume sufficient resources to offset the very goal of trying to make the optimal choice (Laudeman & Palmer, 1995; Raby & Wickens, 1994).

While there are many design-relevant research conclusions in this area, many of these are also based upon only limited data, or data collected in fairly simple laboratory environments. In the following, we describe some of the more important of these.

More optimal task switching can be achieved with a preview of upcoming tasks (e.g., their duration (Tulga & Sheridan, 1980)).

Particularly in widely distributed visual workspaces, task switching can be partially captured by eye movements, using the SEEV model to prescribe optimal switching (Koh et al., 2011, Koh Park & Wickens, 2014).

Very low task switching frequency in multitask environments is suboptimal (Adler & Benbunan-Fich, 2012; Raby & Wickens, 1994; Wickens et al., 2021), and optimal switching frequency can at least partially be dictated by optimal models (Moray, 1986; Wickens et al., 2008).

Very low task switching frequency characterizes what is sometimes referred to as “attentional tunneling” or “attentional narrowing” when tasks served by critical areas of interest are neglected for long periods (as discussed above in section B1), inviting failures to notice key events in those areas (Horrey & Wickens, 2007; Wickens & Alexander, 2009; Wickens & Horrey, 2009), particularly when those events are unexpected (Wickens et al., 2009). In many instances, the “task” that is neglected is often considered the task of maintaining situation awareness.

Three qualitatively different task features tend to induce attentional tunneling, these being extreme levels of interest (such as an engaging cell phone conversation (Horrey et al., 2017; Horrey & Wickens, 2006)), compelling realistic displays (e.g., a 3-D navigational display; Wickens & Alexander, 2009; Wickens & Yeh, 2019), and fault management (Moray & Rotenberg, 1989). Attentional tunneling can be mitigated by salient alarms for neglected tasks, but to be most effective, such alarms should be adaptive and more likely to be activated if automation infers that neglect is taking place (e.g., following a computer assessment of prolonged head-down orientation during vehicle control).

In interruption management, several variables influence the fluency of task resumption (Dismukes & Nowinski, 2007; Grungeiger et al., 2010; Monk et al., 2008; St. John & Smallman, 2008; Trafton & Monk, 2007; Wickens et al., 2021; Wickens & McCarley, 2008). Two variables in particular are the choice of when to leave an ongoing task (after a subgoal has been completed) and whether a “placeholder” is imposed when the ongoing task is left (e.g., a mark on the page where reading stopped), in order to increase the fluency of return to the OT.

Voice communication tasks tend to be particularly intrusive in interruptions, leading to premature abandonment of ongoing tasks of higher priority (McFarlane & Latorella, 2002; Damos, 1997).

There are beginning to be developed design-oriented solutions that can (a) use automation to monitor the progress of certain types of manual work to assess more appropriate times to interrupt (Bailey & Konstan, 2006; Dorneich et al., 2012); (b) provide advanced notification of the importance of the interruption so that the operator can decide whether or not to fully abandon the ongoing task or postpone a switch to the interruption task (Ho et al., 2004); (c) provide visual placeholders, like a flashing cursor, that will support rapid reacquisition of an ongoing task after the switch (Trafton et al., 2005); (d) provide support tools, particularly for situation awareness maintenance during interruptions, such as that described by St. John and Smallman (2008) and (e) provide techniques for breaking through the attentional tunnel if automation infers that this is taking place (St Lot et al., 2020)

A computational model incorporating some of these effects was developed by Wickens, Gutzwiller et al. (2015), and is called **STOM** (strategic task overload management); the “overload” term deriving from the fact that it is primarily in these times when workload imposed by multi-tasking demands is “over the red line” and concurrent performance impossible that task switching and task shedding strategies are invoked. Here then, the multi-task performer must make decisions, explicit or implicit, of which task to choose (to perform) and which tasks to “shed”.

STOM assumes that at any given time, the overloaded multitasker is performing one task of an ensemble, and then decides (at every model iteration) to either continue performing the task (ongoing task: OT), or switch to one of the “waiting” or alternative tasks (AT). To make this decision, all tasks are explicitly or implicitly evaluated on each of four attributes:

● The Salience of task arrival (the arrival of a phone call is more salient than the arrival of an e-mail; corresponding to salience in NSEEV).

● The inherent **interest** in the task (a cause of engagement, as described above)

● The **priority** of the task (either externally assigned, for example, by doctrine, or by a supervisor), or internally generated by the performer.

● The **difficulty** or resource demands of the task.

Based on these four attributes for each task in a multi-task ensemble, STOM computes which task is more “attractive” to be switched to; or to be continued if it is an ongoing task, and then performs a switch to a task, with a frequency proportional to its attractiveness relative to all others in the ensemble. Thus STOM dictates the switching between tasks, very much analogous to SEEV, in switching visual scans between AOIs. Indeed, in an environment when all tasks are visually supported, there will be a high correlation between time on task (STOM) and percentage dwell time (SEEV). But STOM also addresses nonvisual auditory, cognitive and manual tasks. Importantly also, just as SEEV can predict visual tunneling, so STOM can predict more general “cognitive tunneling’, when the performer stays on tasks far longer than optimal, to the detriment of neglected tasks, that may, in fact, be more important (priority), and perhaps safety critical.

STOM has been evaluated in a number of multi-task scenarios on both generic multi-task simulations (Gutzwiller, Wickens & Clegg, 2016; Wickens Gutzwiller et al., 2016 Experiment 1), and more realistic tasks from a business environment (Gilbert & Wickens, 2017) and an astronautspacecraft environment (Wickens et al., 2016 Experiment 2).

## 4. Conclusions

In conclusion, we have discussed four types of attention: **as selective attention**, acquiring information for further processing, either **sequentially**, via scanning, or **in parallel**, when information is superimposed, and particularly as part of a single object, and as **divided attention** in multitasking, here again, either **sequentially** through discrete task switching, or **in parallel**, through continuous resource allocation. All four types, or modes of attention have pronounced realworld contexts within which they operate; all four are undergirded by theories. Here we have tried to highlight both principles and computational models that are spawned by those theories, with the goal of assisting designers to fabricate attention-sensitive design.

These principles and models serve the goal of allowing designers to identify and categorize forms of attentional errors, like failing to recognize the guidance algorithm failure of a self-driving car, or abandoning the altitude-monitoring task in a high-workload cockpit environment. Models can predict the likelihood of such errors, and principles can guide redesign or training to mitigate them. Given that this approach to understanding attention appears productive, there is a great need for further research to validate these predictive models in applied contexts.

## About the Author

**Chris Wickens** has conducted 50 years of research on the applied implications of attention, particularly to aviation display design, and to cognitive modeling. Much of this research was conducted at the Institute of Aviation and Department of Psychology at the University of Illinois. He has written two textbooks.
